title: Inverting the Transform
intro: Getting x(t) back from X(s). In practice that means breaking X(s) into simple fractions and reading each from a table, with the region of convergence deciding which signal each fraction means. The general formula is an integral up a vertical line.

blocks.text: The table to read from

Every transform pair on the earlier pages is a row of the table below, and the inverse is the same table read backwards. Each right-sided pair has a left-sided twin with the opposite sign and the opposite region.
Partial fractions: distinct poles

Take $X(s) = \dfrac{s + 5}{(s+1)(s+3)}$ with the region $\operatorname{Re} s > -1$. Write it as a sum with one fraction per pole: $\dfrac{A}{s+1} + \dfrac{B}{s+3}$. To find $A$, multiply both sides by $(s+1)$ and then set $s = -1$, so the other term disappears:

So $X(s) = 2/(s+1) - 1/(s+3)$ and the region is to the right of both poles, so both pieces are right-sided: $x(t) = 2e^{-t} - e^{-3t}$ for $t \ge 0$. Checks: at $s = 1$, $X = 6/8 = 0.75$ and the fractions give $2/2 - 1/4 = 0.75$. And $x(0) = 2 - 1 = 1$, which the initial value theorem confirms: $sX(s) \to 1$ as $s \to \infty$.
If the numerator has the same degree as the denominator or higher, divide first. $X(s) = (s+3)/(s+1) = 1 + 2/(s+1)$ is $\delta(t) + 2e^{-t}u(t)$: the constant 1 is an impulse.
Repeated poles

$X(s) = \dfrac{1}{(s+1)^2(s+2)}$, region $\operatorname{Re} s > -1$. A double pole needs one fraction for each power: $\dfrac{A}{s+1} + \dfrac{B}{(s+1)^2} + \dfrac{C}{s+2}$. Covering up works for the highest power and for the simple pole: $B = 1/(-1+2) = 1$ and $C = 1/(-2+1)^2 = 1$. For $A$, use the behaviour at large $s$: $X$ falls like $1/s^3$, so the $1/s$ terms must cancel, $A + C = 0$ and $A = -1$. Check at $s = 1$: $X = 1/12 = 0.0833$, and $-1/2 + 1/4 + 1/3 = 0.0833$.

It starts at $x(0) = 0$, as it must, and at $t = 1$ it is $e^{-2} = 0.135$. The $t\,e^{-t}$ is the signature of the double pole, as on the page Pole Positions and the Time Signal (#/math/laplace-transform/poles-and-time).
Complex poles

$X(s) = \dfrac{5}{s(s^2 + 2s + 5)}$, region $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$. The quadratic has roots $-1 \pm j2$, so it is not worth splitting into two complex fractions. Instead keep it whole: $\dfrac{A}{s} + \dfrac{Bs + D}{s^2 + 2s + 5}$. At $s = 0$, $A = 5/5 = 1$. Then $5 = (s^2 + 2s + 5) + (Bs + D)s$ gives $B = -1$ and $D = -2$:
Rewriting $s + 2 = (s + 1) + 1$ makes each piece a table entry with $a = 1$, $\omega_0 = 2$:
At $t = 0$ it is $0$; at $t = 1$ it is $0.986$; it rings around the final value $1$ with an envelope $e^{-t}$ and a period of $\pi = 3.14$ s. The final value theorem agrees: $sX \to 5/5 = 1$.
The ROC picks the signal

The same $X(s)$ with a different region is a different signal, which is why the region is part of the answer. Take $X(s) = \dfrac{1}{(s+1)(s-2)} = \dfrac13\left[\dfrac{1}{s-2} - \dfrac{1}{s+1}\right]$. The poles at $-1$ and $2$ cut the plane into three regions:

items: $\operatorname{Re} s > 2$: both pieces right-sided, $x(t) = \tfrac13\bigl(e^{2t} - e^{-t}\bigr)u(t)$. Causal, but it grows: unstable.

$-1 < \operatorname{Re} s < 2$: the pole at $-1$ is right-sided and the pole at $2$ is left-sided, $x(t) = -\tfrac13 e^{-t}u(t) - \tfrac13 e^{2t}u(-t)$. Two-sided, and it decays in both directions: stable, with a Fourier transform. Not causal.
$\operatorname{Re} s < -1$: both left-sided, $x(t) = \tfrac13\bigl(e^{-t} - e^{2t}\bigr)u(-t)$. Not causal, and it blows up as $t \to -\infty$.

blocks.text: Only the middle one contains the imaginary axis. A transfer function with poles on both sides of the axis can be stable, but only by being non-causal; a causal system has to have every pole to the left.

The viewer's two-sided exponential has $X(s) = 1/(0.25 - s^2) = 1/(s+0.5) - 1/(s-0.5)$: poles at $\pm 0.5$, the strip between them as its region, and in time the right piece $e^{-0.5t}u(t)$ plus the left piece $e^{0.5t}u(-t)$ together make $e^{-0.5|t|}$. Look at the signal panel: it is symmetric and peaks at 1 at $t = 0$. Switch Input signal to decaying exponential: that is the right piece alone, its pole at $-0.5$ and the region a half-plane to the right of it. The left piece is the viewer's left-sided exponential with Decay rate a set to $-0.5$: that signal is $-e^{0.5t}u(-t)$, the left piece with its sign flipped, with the pole at $+0.5$ and the region a half-plane to its left.
The inversion integral
The general formula, for any transform and any region, is the Bromwich integral:

blocks.tex: x(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi j}\int_{c - j\infty}^{c + j\infty} X(s)\, e^{st}\, ds

blocks.text: The path is a vertical line $\operatorname{Re} s = c$, which must lie inside the region of convergence. Think of it as the transform's own definition run backwards: the line $\operatorname{Re} s = c$ is the Fourier transform of $x(t)e^{-ct}$, and the inverse Fourier transform brings back $x(t)e^{-ct}$, after which multiplying by $e^{ct}$ gives $x(t)$. Moving the line within the region changes nothing; moving it out of the region gives the wrong answer, or none.

A numerical test, with $X(s) = 1/(s + 0.5)$. Take $c = 1$ (in the region $\operatorname{Re} s > -0.5$) and integrate up to $\pm 4000$ rad/s: at $t = 1$ the result is $0.6067$, against $e^{-0.5} = 0.6065$, and at $t = -1$ it is $-0.00002$, which is zero. With $c = -1$ instead, which is in the other region $\operatorname{Re} s < -0.5$, the same formula gives $-1.6489$ at $t = -1$, where $-e^{0.5} = -1.6487$, and zero at $t = 1$: the left-sided signal. Same formula, different line, different signal.

To do this integral by hand, close the line into a loop. For $t > 0$, $e^{st}$ shrinks as $\operatorname{Re} s \to -\infty$, so close with a big arc on the left; the integral is then the sum of the residues of $X(s)e^{st}$ at the poles to the left of the line. For $t < 0$ close on the right, with a minus sign from the direction of travel. In the example above with the region $-1 < \operatorname{Re} s < 2$: for $t > 0$ the pole at $-1$ is on the left, with residue $e^{-t}/(-1-2) = -\tfrac13 e^{-t}$; for $t < 0$ the pole at $2$ is on the right, giving $-e^{2t}/(2+1) = -\tfrac13 e^{2t}$. Both agree with the signal above. The residue at a simple pole $p$ is $\lim (s - p)X(s)e^{st}$, which is exactly the cover-up coefficient times $e^{pt}$, so partial fractions are the residue method in disguise.
Problems

blocks.title: A step response
blocks.text: Invert $X(s) = \dfrac{1}{s(s+4)}$, region $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$.
solution: Cover-up: the coefficient of $1/s$ is $1/4$ and that of $1/(s+4)$ is $1/(-4)$. So $X = \tfrac14\left[\dfrac1s - \dfrac1{s+4}\right]$ and $x(t) = \tfrac14\bigl(1 - e^{-4t}\bigr)$. It tends to $0.25$, which is what $sX(s) = 1/(s+4) \to 1/4$ says.

blocks.title: Complex poles
blocks.text: Invert $X(s) = \dfrac{s+3}{s^2 + 2s + 5}$, region $\operatorname{Re} s > -1$.
solution: The poles are $-1 \pm j2$. Complete the square: $s^2 + 2s + 5 = (s+1)^2 + 4$, and $s + 3 = (s+1) + 2$. So $X = \dfrac{s+1}{(s+1)^2 + 4} + \dfrac{2}{(s+1)^2 + 4}$, which is $e^{-t}\cos 2t + e^{-t}\sin 2t$. Check: $x(0) = 1$, and $sX(s) \to 1$.

blocks.title: Pick the region
blocks.text: $X(s) = \dfrac{1}{(s+2)(s-1)}$. Which region gives a signal with a Fourier transform, and what is that signal?
solution: The poles are at $-2$ and $1$; the strip $-2 < \operatorname{Re} s < 1$ contains the imaginary axis. Cover-up: $\dfrac{1}{(s+2)(s-1)} = -\dfrac13\cdot\dfrac{1}{s+2} + \dfrac13\cdot\dfrac{1}{s-1}$. In the strip, the pole at $-2$ is right-sided and the pole at $1$ is left-sided: $x(t) = -\tfrac13 e^{-2t}u(t) - \tfrac13 e^{t}u(-t)$.
